grammar:
?start: omega
?u: gt | lt | err_bnd | d_gt | d_lt | d_err_bnd
gt: s "(t)" ">" c
lt: s "(t)" "<" c
err_bnd: "abs(" s "(t)" "-" c ")" "<" e
d_gt: "d_" s "(t)" ">" D_C
d_lt: "d_" s "(t)" "<" D_C
d_err_bnd: "abs(" "d_" s "(t)" "-" D_C ")" "<" e
?e: ERROR | /[0-9]+/ | /[0-9]+.[0-9]+/ 
ERROR: "e"
c: s "(" t_a ")" | C_LOW | C_MID | C_HIGH
C_LOW: "c(low)"
C_MID: "c(mid)"
C_HIGH: "c(high)"
D_C : "0" | "d_c(low)" | "d_c(high)" | "-d_c(low)" | "-d_c(high)"
?phi: u | u_and_phi
?nu : u | u_implies_u | u_and_phi
u_implies_u: u "→" u
u_and_phi: u "^" phi | u "∧" phi
?psi: temp_op_fg | temp_op_g | temp_op_f
temp_op_fg: "F" "[" t_a "," t_a "]" "G" "(" nu ")"
temp_op_f: "F" "[" t_a "," t_a "]" "(" nu ")"
temp_op_g: "G" "[" t_a "," t_a "]" "(" nu ")"
?omega: nu | psi | omega "^" omega | omega "∧" omega | psi "→" psi
t_a: /[0-9]+/ | "infinity" | "inf" | /∞/
s: /[\w]+/
d_s: /d_[\w]+/
%import common.WS
%ignore WS
core_prompt_1: Translate the following natural language statement into a signal temporal logic (STL) statement:
core_prompt_2:
Format your response in JSON. Include (1) your thinking, (2) the input statement, (3) your STL response, and (4) an explanation of how the input statement and STL output are related.

Your STL response must conform to these rules:
[BEGIN RULES]
u : less_than | greater_than | close_to_value | derivative_greater_than | derivative_less_than | derivative_close_to_value
less_than : s(t) < c # Species s is less than value c
greater_than : s(t) > c # Species s is greater than value c
close_to_value : abs(s(t) - c) < e # Species s is within a small margin e of value c
derivative_greater_than : d_s(t) > d_c # The rate of change species s is greater than value d_c
derivative_less_than : d_s(t) < d_c # The rate of change of species s is less than value d_c
derivative_close_to_value : abs(d_s(t) - d_c) < e # The rate of change species s is is within a small margin e of value d_c
e : "e" | [0-9]+ # e is a small error margin specified as either a concrete number or just left as the variable e
c : s(t_a) | "c(low)" | "c(mid)" | "c(high)" # c is the level of a species, it can be a specific value or generally just low, moderate, or high
d_c : 0 # Rate of change is 0
	| "d_c(low)" # Species is slowly increasing
	| "d_c(high)" # Species is rapidly increasing
	| "-d_c(low)" # Species is slowly decreasing
	| "-d_c(high)" # Species is quickly decreasing
phi : u | u1 ^ u2 | u1 → u2 # You can combine smaller conditions using Boolean and (^) and implication (→) 
psi : eventually[t_a,t_b]globally(phi) # This temporal operator means that between day a and b, there is a point at which condition phi becomes true for the rest of the interval
	| globally[t_a,t_b](phi) # This temporal operator means that condition phi is true over the entire interval from day a to b
	| eventually[t_a,t_b](phi) # This temporal operator that means there is at least 1 time between days a and b that some condition phi is true
t_a : number | ∞ # Days can be specified as a concrete integer and if an end day is not specified then infinity can be used
s : IL6 | IL12 | IL1β | IL1Ra | TNFα | IL8 | IFNα | IFNβ | SARSCoV2 | IL1RN # These are the species names you can use
d_IL6 | d_IL12 | d_IL1β | d_IL1Ra | d_TNFα | d_IL8 | d_IFNα | d_IFNβ | d_SARSCoV2 | d_IL1RN # These are the names for the derivatives of the species
[END RULES]

The d_s terms represent the derivative of a signal, so you may find those terms helpful for describing how signals increase or decrease. For general statements describing the levels of some species as "high" or "low" for example, you may find comparison statements helpful.
